paras.text: Contract Literacy & Landmine Clauses — Audio Lecture

This chapter is different from everything else in this track. Every other chapter is Michigan insurance law: policies, appraisal, bad faith, adjuster licensing. This one steps back and asks a more basic question. How do you read any contract, a GC subcontract, a vendor agreement, a lease, a work authorization, without getting burned by a clause buried in paragraph nine that quietly changes everything.
Nine landmine clauses, in order. A method for reading anything you sign, not just an insurance policy.
Idea one. The merger clause, and the fraud exception that is almost dead.

Most contracts end with a boring-looking sentence saying the written document is the entire agreement. That is a merger clause, also called an integration clause. It sounds like throwaway boilerplate. It is not.

The controlling Michigan case is UAW-GM Human Resource Center versus KSL Recreation Corporation, Michigan Court of Appeals, March sixth, nineteen ninety eight, published. The court held that when the parties include an integration clause in their written contract, it is conclusive. And it nullifies all antecedent agreements, meaning everything said or promised before signing.

Here is the part that should worry you. Normally, before deciding whether a contract is the whole deal, a court can look at outside evidence of what was said beforehand. UAW-GM holds that a valid merger clause skips that step entirely. The only way around it is fraud, and the court narrowed that exception almost to nothing. The only fraud that can still undo the contract is fraud relating to the merger clause itself, or fraud that invalidates the entire contract, merger clause included.

Translate that into a job site. A superintendent verbally promises your crew extra pay if mold turns up. You sign a one-page work order with a merger clause at the bottom. Mold turns up. The verbal promise is gone, unless the fraud was about the merger clause itself. The fix is getting it in writing before you sign, not arguing about it afterward.

Question. A verbal promise was made before signing, and the signed contract has a merger clause and says nothing about that promise. What single word determines whether you can still enforce it, and what does it have to attach to?

The word is fraud, and it has to attach to the merger clause itself, or to the entire contract including the merger clause. A general claim that someone lied about some other fact during negotiation is not enough.
Idea two. Indemnify, defend, and hold harmless are three different promises, not one.
Contracts love to bundle these three words into a single sentence, shall indemnify, defend, and hold harmless, as if they were interchangeable. They are not.

Indemnify means pay for an established loss, in dollars, after the loss is determined. Defend means fund or provide the actual defense, usually legal costs, while a claim is still pending, before anyone knows who owes what. Hold harmless is generally treated as functionally the same as indemnify, a promise not to pursue the other party for the loss. That is general commentary, not a Michigan court holding.

Michigan authority on how far apart indemnify and defend can be comes out of insurance law, where it gets litigated the most. American Bumper and Manufacturing Company versus Hartford Fire Insurance Company, Michigan Supreme Court, nineteen ninety six, held that the scope of the two duties is not identical, and the duty to defend is broader than the duty to indemnify. Auto Owners Insurance Company versus City of Clare, Michigan Supreme Court, nineteen ninety four, says the same thing and explains why: the duty to defend is triggered even arguably within the coverage, and arises in instances in which coverage is even arguable, though the claim may be groundless or frivolous.

Be honest about the limit here. Both cases are about an insurer defending its own policyholder, not a GC-subcontractor dispute. No Michigan case applying that exact rule outside insurance was found this session. Use the logic, defend can be owed before and independent of indemnify, but do not borrow those case names for a commercial fight. That is practitioner reasoning, not a cited holding.

Picture a mitigation sub whose contract says it shall indemnify, defend, and hold harmless the GC for claims from its work. A homeowner slips on wet flooring the sub left uncovered and sues the GC. Before fault is ever decided, defend can require the sub to fund the GC's legal defense right now. Indemnify is the separate, later question of who pays if there is a judgment. A sub who reads only indemnify misses that defend can bite immediately.
Idea three. Limitation of liability, and the carve-outs that survive anyway.

A limitation of liability clause caps the dollar amount one side can collect from the other, or excludes a category like consequential damages, the knock-on losses beyond the direct cost of fixing something. Michigan's enactment of the Uniform Commercial Code, M C L four forty point twenty seven nineteen, lets parties limit remedies, and treats an agreed remedy as merely optional unless the contract expressly makes it exclusive, in which case it is the sole remedy. Two guardrails matter. If an exclusive remedy fails of its essential purpose, meaning it turns out worthless in practice, the statute reopens ordinary remedies. And consequential damages can be limited unless the limitation is unconscionable, with personal injury limits on consumer goods presumed unconscionable, while commercial-loss limits are not.

That is the UCC side. There is a separate doctrine for clauses that try to waive liability for negligence outright. Xu versus Gay, Michigan Court of Appeals, two thousand three, held that a contractual waiver of liability also serves to insulate against ordinary negligence, but not gross negligence. The court defined gross negligence as conduct so reckless as to demonstrate a substantial lack of concern for whether an injury results.

Put the two together. A cap on ordinary contract damages can hold up to UCC limits. A clause wiping out liability entirely for gross negligence, willful misconduct, or fraud runs into Xu's line, and a good limitation clause writes its own carve-out for exactly those categories.

Picture a rented dehumidifier. An ordinary thermostat failure causing a fire, the cap probably holds. A technician who deliberately disables a known safety shutoff to make the unit work better, and that choice starts the fire, looks like conduct a court could call grossly negligent, and Xu says the cap should not protect the company from that.
Question. What is the difference between a UCC damages cap and a clause trying to waive liability for negligence outright, and which one survives gross negligence under Michigan law?

The UCC cap, under M C L four forty point twenty seven nineteen, limits the measure of damages and has its own unconscionability guardrails. A negligence waiver is a separate doctrine, and under Xu versus Gay, it cannot reach gross negligence or willful and wanton misconduct no matter how it is worded.
Idea four. Conditions precedent versus covenants, and why the difference decides whether you even have a claim.

A covenant is a plain promise. Contractor shall complete the roof by June first. Break it, and that is a breach, full stop. A condition precedent is different. Harbor Park Market versus Gronda, Michigan Court of Appeals, two thousand seven, defines it as a fact or event that the parties intend must take place before there is a right to performance. If that event never happens, there may be no breach claim at all, because the obligation never came into existence in the first place.

Words like subject to, provided that, on condition that, and if and only if signal a condition. A plain shall or will signals a covenant. In Harbor Park Market itself, the purchase agreement was subject to review and approval of a named attorney by a certain date. Both the trial court and the parties read that as a condition precedent, and the Court of Appeals agreed the clause's own wording compelled it. But the court also said Michigan courts are not inclined to construe contract stipulations as conditions precedent unless the clear language compels it. So this is not a blanket rule that subject to always means a condition. It depends on the actual wording.

On a real job, a mitigation contract that says payment is due subject to the carrier's approval of the estimate, if that is a condition precedent and the carrier never approves it, may leave the contractor with no breach claim at all, because the triggering event never happened. A contractor who wants to be paid regardless needs a plain covenant instead: homeowner shall pay within thirty days of completion.
Idea five. Time is of the essence, and what flipping that switch actually does.

Michigan's default rule, from MacRitchie versus Plumb, Michigan Court of Appeals, nineteen seventy six, is that time is not to be regarded as of the essence of a contract unless made so by express provision of the parties. Time can also become essential by the nature of the contract itself, or by the circumstances under which it was signed.

Without that language, missing a completion date is ordinarily a minor breach. The other side can claim delay damages, but the contract stays in force. Put a time-is-of-the-essence clause in, and that default flips. A missed deadline, even a short one, can become a material breach, meaning the other side can walk away from the whole deal and sue, instead of just collecting delay damages while staying bound.

This gets loaded fast in restoration work, where completion dates interact with insurance deadlines, mortgage inspections, and additional living expense coverage running out on a calendar. A contractor who agrees to that language hands the homeowner, or the carrier behind the homeowner, a sharper tool: a single missed interim deadline can become grounds to terminate.
Question. Same five-day delay on a rebuild, once with no time clause and once with a time-is-of-the-essence clause. What is different, and which case sets the default you are flipping?

Without the clause, MacRitchie versus Plumb's default treats the five days as a minor breach, delay damages only, contract stays alive. With the clause, the same five days can be argued as a material breach, opening the door to termination. The clause is what flips it.
Idea six. Fee-shifting clauses, and the American Rule they are shifting away from.

The default in American litigation, Michigan included, is that each side pays its own lawyer no matter who wins. That is the American Rule. Great Lakes Shores versus Bartley, Michigan Court of Appeals, two thousand fifteen, states it plainly: attorney fees are not recoverable from a losing party unless authorized by a statute, court rule, or other recognized exception. And it confirms a written fee-shifting clause in a contract is exactly that kind of exception. Such contractual provisions are enforceable.

Read the direction of the clause before you sign it. A mutual, prevailing-party clause lets whichever side wins collect fees from the loser, which pushes both sides toward settling a marginal dispute instead of fighting it. A one-way clause, common in agreements the stronger party writes, lets only one named side collect fees if it wins, and exposes the other side to that bill regardless of who actually wins. A referral-network agreement that says contractor shall pay company's attorney fees in any dispute, with nothing about the company ever paying the contractor's fees, is exactly that kind of one-way exposure.
Idea seven. Venue, forum selection, and jury waivers.

A forum-selection clause picks the court system, and often the state, where a dispute has to be filed. A venue clause picks the specific county within that system. Michigan has a real statute backing this up for clauses pointing out of state, M C L six hundred point seven forty five. Subsection three says that when the parties agreed in writing to litigate only in another state, and someone files in Michigan anyway, the court shall dismiss or stay the action, unless one of five listed exceptions applies: a statute requires Michigan to hear it, the plaintiff cannot get effective relief elsewhere, the other state is substantially less convenient, the clause was obtained by misrepresentation or duress or unconscionable means, or enforcing it would otherwise be unfair.

Turcheck versus Amerifund Financial, Michigan Court of Appeals, two thousand six, summarizes the policy behind that statute: Michigan courts generally enforce contractual forum-selection clauses as written, and Michigan's public policy favors enforcing them, unless one of those statutory exceptions applies.

Jury-trial waivers are a related but separate clause, giving up the right to a jury and leaving the facts to a judge alone. A Michigan Court of Appeals case from two thousand eighteen is commonly cited for enforcing these, but I could not open the actual opinion at a confirmed address this session, so I will not quote it or put a holding in your mouth. What is safe to say, resting on the same enforce-unambiguous-language reasoning Michigan applies to contracts generally, is that a clearly worded jury waiver tends to be enforced as written, and deserves the same careful read as a forum-selection clause.

Picture a commercial property owner's standard work order, forum clause pointing out of state, jury waiver in the same paragraph. Sign that without reading it, and you have agreed in advance to travel out of state and argue in front of a judge alone if a change-order dispute ever goes to court, a combination that can make a modest dispute too expensive to even pursue.
Idea eight. Including is not a closed list.

In ordinary English and in most contract drafting, the word including introduces examples, not the only items. Covered losses include fire, wind, and theft usually means those are examples of a bigger category, not the complete list, unless the contract says including, and limited to, or including only. This is a general drafting canon, not a Michigan statute or a case holding verified this session, and it cuts both directions. A scope-of-work clause that says the price includes labor, materials, and equipment rental does not automatically exclude an unlisted item like dumpster fees, but it does not automatically include it either. The fix is drafting a genuinely closed list up front, not arguing about the canon after the dispute starts.
Idea nine. Shall, may, and will, and the ambiguity sloppy drafting creates.

Shall signals a mandatory obligation. May signals a permissive option, allowed but not required. Will is grammatically a statement about the future, and careful drafters avoid using it to create a duty at all.

Manuel versus Gill, Michigan Supreme Court, two thousand eight, endorses the shall and may default directly: the term may is permissive, as opposed to the term shall, which is considered mandatory. That case construes a statute, not a private contract, so treat its use here as the right general default, not a direct contract-law holding. No Michigan contract case on will specifically was found this session; that point stays general drafting commentary.

The real danger is a contract that mixes all three in similar-looking clauses. Contractor shall begin work within twenty four hours. Homeowner may cancel within three business days. Contractor will submit a final invoice within ten days. Read carefully, shall and may are doing different, deliberate jobs. Will is the odd one out, and a careful reader should ask whether the drafter actually meant shall there, or was just being careless.

Recap, fast, the way to hold all nine in your head on any job with paperwork. A merger clause erases what was said before signing, and only narrow fraud about the clause itself gets it back. Indemnify, defend, and hold harmless are three separate promises in one sentence, and defend can hit before indemnify ever does. A limitation of liability clause can cap ordinary damages but not gross negligence, willful misconduct, or fraud. A condition precedent means no right to performance exists until the triggering event happens, sharper than a covenant's ordinary breach. Time is of the essence flips a missed deadline into a possible material breach. A fee-shifting clause is a real exception to the American Rule, and the direction it points matters. A forum-selection clause backed by M C L six hundred point seven forty five is enforced as written absent one of five exceptions, and a jury waiver next to it raises the stakes further. Including is non-exhaustive by default, cutting both ways. And shall, may, and will are supposed to mean three different things, not one careless habit.

Read every contract in that order, merger clause first, risk-and-money clauses second, claim-triggering clauses third, cost-and-forum clauses fourth, small words last, and you will catch the landmine before it catches you.
